chapters.title: Build upward
chapters.text: Begin overhead, then tilt: functions can be stacked rather than placed side by side, shortening selected die-to-die routes. This is not a stack of circuit boards. Dies meet at carefully controlled interfaces. Count the layers and identify what each layer contributes before inspecting the bond.

chapters.title: Assign the layers
chapters.text: Upper and lower dies can divide compute, memory and connection functions in different ways. Their process technologies need not match. This is a generic teaching model, not an internal floorplan of a particular SoIC or Foveros product. Architecture determines which functions belong together.

chapters.title: Two bonds at one interface
chapters.text: Approach the interface: copper contacts provide electrical connections while surrounding dielectric surfaces also bond. That combination defines hybrid bonding. Do not picture a row of large solder balls. Solder microbumps and direct hybrid bonding are different interconnect approaches with different integration constraints.

chapters.title: Prepare before aligning
chapters.text: Separate the dies and imagine a particle or uneven surface trapped between them. Surface preparation, cleanliness, flatness and alignment work together to determine bond quality. The motion is slowed to explain the principle; it is not a cleaning recipe or a manufacturing temperature schedule.

chapters.title: Separate contact from route
chapters.text: The bond interface is short, but data still traverses circuits and wiring within each die. Vertical connectivity solves only part of the path; it does not remove logic delay. Identify the crossing between dies, then place that crossing back into the complete signal chain.

chapters.title: Turn density into system value
chapters.text: Dense contacts can support richer communication between layers, but the architecture must make use of them. Define the division of data and work before allocating contacts and power. More connections are not a goal by themselves. Animated movement shows information relationships, not a claimed transfer speed.

chapters.title: Heat beneath the stack
chapters.text: From the side, follow heat out of the stack. Heat-source location, interface resistance and cooler placement jointly affect temperature. A taller stack is not automatically better. Where the hottest circuits belong is an architectural decision to make early, not a problem to postpone until assembly.

chapters.title: Test before burying a die
chapters.text: Contacts become difficult to reach after another die covers them, so test access must be designed in advance. Pre-assembly screening, post-bond connectivity and system testing serve different purposes. One passing test is not a permanent guarantee; coverage and remaining risk must be explicit.

chapters.title: Density, yield and repair
chapters.text: Zoom out: dense integration makes interface quality and test planning more important. Bonded dies may not be economical to replace, increasing the value of earlier screening. Compare solutions using cost per good unit, thermal conditions and repair options together, rather than connection density alone.

chapters.title: Return from stack to system
chapters.text: The route is functional partitioning, interface design, surface preparation, alignment, bonding, testability and thermal verification. The aim of 3D is not merely a taller building. It is to bring communicating functions closer while preserving dependable paths for electricity, heat and testing.
